title: Walsenburg Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Walsenburg wells have a 30-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock makes yield and drilling cost vary widely.
h1: Walsenburg Colorado Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
Buying land near Walsenburg means looking past the advertised presence of a well. The local record includes 596 permitted wells, but only 367 are recorded as constructed, 402 report total depth, 49 report pump yield, and 31 report static water level. That uneven record matters: the numbers are useful for setting expectations, but they do not replace a pump test, water-quality testing, or a review of the actual permit.

Most permits identify unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers rather than a consistently mapped production zone. Conditions can change quickly across mountain ground, including around La Veta, Lynn, Aguilar, Colorado City, Rye, and Gardner. Check the specific neighboring wells before committing to a lot.

sections.heading: Walsenburg well depth depends on the local bedrock
sections.html:
The reported median well depth near Walsenburg is 30 feet, and the middle half runs from 20 to 100 feet. That shallow median should not be treated as a guaranteed drilling target. The record reaches 400 feet at the 90th percentile and 1,838 feet at the deepest recorded well. About 74% of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 11% fall in the 100-to-300-foot range, another 11% in the 300-to-600-foot range, and 4% exceed 600 feet.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer: 564 wells do so. In fractured granite and gneiss, water can travel through separate fractures rather than a uniform layer. For a bid, ask the driller to explain the price per foot, casing and grout assumptions, and what happens if the first hole does not produce.

sections.heading: What Walsenburg wells produce for a household
sections.html:
Among the 49 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 4.0 to 10.5 gallons per minute. The distribution is generally encouraging for ordinary household use: 63% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, 24% report 1 to 5, and 10% report more than 15. Only 2% report under 1 gallon per minute.

These are reported well yields, not a promise for an unbuilt well or proof of sustained household supply. A buyer should ask how the yield was measured and request the well construction and pump records. A low-producing well may still serve a home with adequate storage, while a higher reported yield does not remove the need for water-quality testing and maintenance planning.

sections.heading: The recorded water level shows a change worth investigating
sections.html:
The overall median static water level is 22 feet below surface, with the middle half from 10 to 144 feet. The decade figures show a substantial difference: the median measured level was 10 feet below surface in the 2010s and 164 feet below surface in the 2020s.

That pattern suggests the recorded water table or measured well levels may be deeper in the newer decade, but it is not enough by itself to prove a basin-wide decline. Only 31 wells report static water level, and the wells may differ in location, construction, aquifer, and measurement conditions. Before buying, compare nearby well logs and ask for a current measurement from the property well. A driller or water professional can help determine whether the change reflects local fractures, pumping, seasonal conditions, or a broader trend.

sections.heading: Permit history shows continued activity near Walsenburg
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records show permits from the 1960s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. Permit counts were 5 in the 1960s, 6 in the 1970s, 11 in the 1980s, 107 in the 1990s, 125 in the 2000s, 174 in the 2010s, and 64 in the 2020s. The totals describe permits issued by decade, not necessarily completed wells or currently operating systems.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 203 records, Timber Line Drilling (Pfaffenhauser, Robert G.) with 32, and Boday Well Drilling (Boday, Kathleen) with 24. Confirm current licensing, availability, insurance, and the scope of work directly before selecting a contractor. A permit record also does not confirm that a particular well is legal for every intended use.

sections.heading: Budgeting a new well in Walsenburg
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, at roughly $65 to $100 per foot. At the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,000 to $3,000. That is only the drilling portion. A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $8,000 to $15,000.

Depth is the largest obvious variable, but access, casing, grout, drilling conditions, water storage, electrical distance, and difficult fractures can change the final bid. Ask for a written allowance for each item and clarify whether testing, permit work, abandonment of a dry hole, and site restoration are included. The deepest recorded well is 1,838 feet, showing why a median-based budget should not be treated as a ceiling.

sections.heading: Check water quality, mining history, and the building site
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 88 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those flags do not prove that a particular parcel has contaminated water, but they justify testing based on the property location, well construction, and nearby land uses. Test before closing and use a qualified laboratory.

Low yield, an unsuccessful hole, or a deep water level can affect both cost and house design. Confirm the well permit, production capacity, water quality, and setback requirements before placing the house, septic system, driveway, or outbuildings. Septic soil conditions and separation from the well also matter. Ask the county and DWR about allowable household use, and remember that an exempt household-use well has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit and may face water-right restrictions in an over-appropriated basin.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Walsenburg?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Walsenburg is 30 feet, with the middle half from 20 to 100 feet. About 74% are under 100 feet. Conditions vary sharply in fractured mountain bedrock, however: the 90th percentile is 400 feet and the deepest recorded well is 1,838 feet. Neighboring well logs are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Walsenburg?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses about $65 to $100 per foot. At the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,000 to $3,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,000 to $15,000. Fractured granite or gneiss, access, depth, and dry-hole risk can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Walsenburg?
faq.a: Among 49 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 4.0 to 10.5. About 63% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 2% report under 1. These figures describe recorded wells, not a guarantee for a new hole. Request a pump test and review storage capacity.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Walsenburg?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or a nearby well’s yield. Within about 10 miles, records show 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 88 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test the actual property well through a qualified laboratory, with testing selected for local conditions and the parcel’s nearby land uses.

faq.q: Are Walsenburg well levels getting lower?
faq.a: The recorded median static water level was 10 feet below surface in the 2010s and 164 feet below surface in the 2020s. That difference deserves investigation, but only 31 wells report static water levels, and the wells may differ in location and construction. It suggests a possible deeper water level in newer measurements, not proof of a region-wide decline.
